claims.claim: Over-expression of Kr in post-mitotic neurons is sufficient to drive changes in ion channel gene expression.
claims.source: Furthermore, over-expression of Kr in post-mitotic neurons is sufficient to drive changes in ion channel gene expression (Parrish et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claims.claim: When Kr and Shal are simultaneously knocked down in MN1, firing rates were significantly decreased compared to wild type at all current steps above 25 pA.
claims.source: However, when Kr and Shal are simultaneously knocked down in MN1, firing rates were significantly decreased compared to wild type at all current steps above 25 pA (Figure 3A & B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: Induction of Kr expression following loss of Shal is required for FRH.
claims.source: These data are consistent with the conclusion that induction of Kr expression following loss of Shal is required for FRH.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing impaired FRH when Kr is knocked down.

claims.claim: Firing rates are equivalent when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Shal RNAi animals.
claims.source: Firing rates are equivalent when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Shal RNAi animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Firing rates are unchanged when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Kr RNAi animals.
claims.source: Firing rates are also unchanged when comparing wild type and MN1-GAL4 > Kr RNAi animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Post mitotic knockdown of Kr has no baseline effect on firing rates.
claims.source: This is an important control, demonstrating that post mitotic knockdown of Kr, a master regulator of cell fate in the embryo, has no baseline effect.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing no change in firing rates with Kr-RNAi alone.

claims.claim: In the Shal-RNAi condition, action potential (AP) waveforms are indistinguishable from wild type.
claims.source: In the Shal-RNAi condition, action potential (AP) waveforms are indistinguishable from wild type, arguing for preservation of AP waveform during FRH (Figure 3C,D & E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, D, and E.

claims.claim: Kr-RNAi has no effect on AP waveform.
claims.source: We found that Kr-RNAi has no effect on AP waveform.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of action potential waveform parameters.

claims.claim: When Shal and Kr were simultaneously knocked down in MN1, AP waveforms were significantly altered.
claims.source: However, when Shal and Kr were simultaneously knocked down in MN1, AP waveforms were significantly altered (Figure 3C & D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The after-hyperpolarization amplitude was significantly smaller and AP half-width duration was significantly increased in double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi compared to wild type.
claims.source: Specifically, the after-hyperpolarization amplitude was significantly smaller and AP half-width duration was significantly increased compared to wild type.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of action potential waveform parameters.

claims.claim: Kr participates in homeostatic control of both action potential waveform and firing rates following loss of Shal.
claims.source: Thus, Kr participates in homeostatic control of both action potential waveform and firing rates following loss of Shal.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing altered AP waveform and firing rates when Kr is knocked down.

claims.claim: Kr is a master regulator of cell fate determination in neurons.
claims.source: It is well established that Kr is a master regulator of cell fate determination in neurons (Isshiki et al., 2001) and other cell types (McConnell and Yang, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Isshiki et al., 2001 and McConnell and Yang, 2010.

claims.claim: There was no change in MN1 cell number or gross morphology in the CNS across the four genotypes examined.
claims.source: There was no change in MN1 cell number or gross morphology in the CNS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B,C & D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: No significant differences in somatic diameter and proximal dendrite width were observed across the four genotypes.
claims.source: We further measured somatic diameter and the width of the proximal dendrite as features that contribute to the passive electrical properties of these cells. No significant differences were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E & F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E and F.

claims.claim: A decrease in input resistance was found for both Kr-RNAi and combined Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi.
claims.source: Finally, we quantified cell capacitance and input resistance (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G & H). We found a decrease in input resistance for both Kr-RNAi and combined Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H.

claims.claim: The double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition had the highest variability of all four genotypes for current steps above 100 pA.
claims.source: The double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition had the highest variability of all four genotypes, an effect that is not additive for current steps above 100 pA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of coefficient of variation across cells.

claims.claim: No individual cell in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition ever fired at rates exceeding wild type.
claims.source: Finally, it is worth noting that no individual cell ever fired at rates exceeding wild type as we observe following application of 4-AP (Figure 1D), indicating that the loss of firing rate homeostasis is not without some remaining constraint on firing frequencies in vivo.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations comparing individual cell firing rates.

claims.claim: The increase in IKCa following loss of Shal was completely blocked by simultaneous Kr knockdown.
claims.source: Here, we demonstrate that the increase in IKCa following loss of Shal was completely blocked by simultaneous Kr knockdown (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Kr knockdown had no effect on baseline IKCa.
claims.source: Importantly, Kr knockdown had no effect on baseline IKCa (Figure 5D) or on voltage-gated calcium currents in the Shal-RNAi background (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Kr knockdown had no effect on voltage-gated calcium currents in the Shal-RNAi background.
claims.source: Importantly, Kr knockdown had no effect on baseline IKCa (Figure 5D) or on voltage-gated calcium currents in the Shal-RNAi background (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Kr is required for the homeostatic enhancement of IKCa.
claims.source: Thus, Kr is required for the homeostatic enhancement of IKCa.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing blocked IKCa enhancement when Kr is knocked down.

claims.claim: Kr is the first gene demonstrated to have a selective action for homeostatic changes in channel function, without altering baseline channel activity.
claims.source: To our knowledge, Kr is the first gene demonstrated to have a selective action for homeostatic changes in channel function, without altering baseline channel activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing Kr's specific role in homeostatic regulation.

claims.claim: IKDR remained elevated in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition, similar to that observed in Shal-RNAi alone.
claims.source: Next, we examined IKDR. We found that IKDR remained elevated in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition (Figure 5A), similar to that observed in Shal-RNAi alone (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and comparison to Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Kr does not control the homeostatic upregulation of IKDR following loss of Shal.
claims.source: This suggests that Kr does not control the homeostatic upregulation of IKDR following loss of Shal.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing maintained IKDR elevation without Kr.

claims.claim: Kr knockdown alone had no effect on baseline IKDR.
claims.source: We confirmed that Kr knockdown alone had no effect on baseline IKDR (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: IKA was knocked down just as efficiently in double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi neurons as when Shal-RNAi was driven alone.
claims.source: Finally, as another control, we quantified IKA in double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi neurons and demonstrate that IKA was knocked down just as efficiently as when Shal-RNAi was driven alone (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Loss of Kr participates in a specific facet of FRH induced by loss of Shal.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that loss of Kr participates in a specific facet of FRH induced by loss of Shal.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing Kr's selective control of IKCa.

claims.claim: Bath application of paxilline (600 nM) to both wild-type and Shal-RNAi preparations significantly reduced firing rates in MN1.
claims.source: We bath applied the selective BK channel inhibitor paxilline (600 nM) to both wild-type and Shal-RNAi preparations, and observed significantly reduced firing rates in MN1 (Figure 6A,B & C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, B, and C.

claims.claim: Paxilline reduced maximal firing rates by 34% on average.
claims.source: Paxilline reduced maximal firing rates by 34% on average, compared to the 12% reduction due to driving Kr-RNAi in the Shal-RNAi background.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of firing rates with paxilline application.

claims.claim: Driving Kr-RNAi in the Shal-RNAi background reduced maximal firing rates by 12%.
claims.source: Paxilline reduced maximal firing rates by 34% on average, compared to the 12% reduction due to driving Kr-RNAi in the Shal-RNAi background.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of firing rates in the double RNAi condition.

claims.claim: Paxilline application resulted in decreased AHP amplitude and a larger AP half-width duration.
claims.source: The effects of paxilline on action potential waveform were also consistent with those seen in the double Shal-RNAi, Kr-RNAi condition. We observed decreased AHP amplitude and a larger AP half-width duration (Figure 5D & E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: Loss of Slo-dependent AP repolarization leads to a broader action potential and shallower AHP, which impedes recovery of sodium channels from inactivation and causes decreased firing rate.
claims.source: Loss of Slo-dependent AP repolarization leads to the observed broader action potential and shallower AHP, an effect that is predicted to impede recovery of sodium channels from inactivation and thus cause decreased firing rate.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results and known biophysical properties of sodium channels.

claims.claim: Upregulation of IKDR occurs in ShalW362F.
claims.source: First, we demonstrate upregulation of IKDR in ShalW362F (Figure 7A), consistent with this expectation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: No significant change in IKCa was found in ShalW362F.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found no significant change in IKCa (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Slo transcript is upregulated following loss of Shal protein.
claims.source: We confirmed, via quantitative PCR, that Slo transcript is upregulated following loss of Shal protein (Figure 7E; see Parrish et al., 2014 for initial observation).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7E and citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claims.claim: No change in Slo transcript was observed in the ShalW362F non-conducting mutant.
claims.source: However, we did not observe a change in Slo transcript in the ShalW362F non-conducting mutant (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: A small but statistically significant broadening of the AP waveform was observed in ShalW362F.
claims.source: In agreement, we observed a small but statistically significant broadening of the AP waveform in ShalW362F (Figure 7C & D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claims.claim: FRH appears to be differentially achieved in ShalW362F compared to Shal-RNAi.
claims.source: Thus, FRH appears to be differentially achieved in ShalW362F compared to Shal-RNAi.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing different compensatory mechanisms.

claims.claim: The transcripts for Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab are significantly elevated in the shal null mutant (Shal495).
claims.source: The transcripts for all four of these genes are significantly elevated in the shal null mutant (Shal495; Parrish et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The transcription of Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab was increased in the Shal null mutant.
claims.source: Confirming prior observations using gene expression arrays (Parrish et al., 2014), the transcription all four genes was increased in the Shal null mutant (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7E and citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claims.claim: None of the genes Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab showed altered expression in ShalW362F.
claims.source: However, none of these genes showed altered expression in ShalW362F (Figure 7F, bottom).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: There was no change in the expression of KCNQ, Shaw and Shawl in ShalW362F.
claims.source: We then extended this analysis in ShalW362F to include KCNQ, Shaw and Shawl (Figure 7F, top). Again, there was no change in the expression of these channels, whereas KCNQ was upregulated in the Shal null (Parrish et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7F and citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claims.claim: KCNQ was upregulated in the Shal null.
claims.source: Again, there was no change in the expression of these channels, whereas KCNQ was upregulated in the Shal null (Parrish et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parrish et al., 2014.

claims.claim: All wild-type and ShalW362F flies climbed up the walls of a glass vial above 10 cm within 10 s.
claims.source: All wild-type and ShalW362F flies climbed up the walls of a glass vial above 10 cm within 10 s.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claims.claim: No statistically significant differences in average climbing speed were detected between wild-type and ShalW362F flies.
claims.source: No statistically significant differences in average climbing speed were detected, consistent with the idea that FRH enables normal motor behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal Shal knockdown (elav-Gal4; Shal-RNAi) dramatically altered animal behavior, and every animal tested failed to ascend past the 10 cm mark within 30 s.
claims.source: Instead, pan-neuronal Shal knockdown dramatically altered animal behavior, and every animal that was tested failed to ascend past the 10 cm mark within 30 s, the maximal allotted time.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claims.claim: Control animals (Shal-RNAi/+) were no different from wild type in climbing behavior.
claims.source: Control animals (Shal-RNAi/+) were no different from wild type.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claims.claim: Motoneuron-specific Shal knockdown (OK371-Gal4) resulted in wild type climbing behavior.
claims.source: As a further control, we assessed motoneuron-specific Shal knockdown (OK371-Gal4). In this experiment, climbing behavior was wild type, again consistent with the conclusion that FRH, which we demonstrate in motoneurons, is sufficient to restore normal animal behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data.

claims.claim: FRH induced by pan-neuronal knockdown of Shal interferes with the subsequent induction of presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) at the neuromuscular junction.
claims.source: We previously demonstrated that FRH, induced by pan-neuronal knockdown of Shal, interferes with the subsequent induction of presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP), assayed at the neuromuscular junction (Bergquist et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bergquist et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Increased Shaker expression blocks the expression of PHP that is selectively induced at the NMJ.
claims.source: A current model for this interference effect is that increased Shaker expression, caused by the presence of the protein null Shal495 mutation or by direct over-expression of a Shaker transgene, blocks the expression of PHP that is selectively induced at the NMJ (Figure 7I & J; Bergquist et al., 2010; Parrish et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bergquist et al., 2010 and Parrish et al., 2014, and reference to Figure 7I and J.

claims.claim: Increased levels of Shaker channel prevent ENaC channel-dependent depolarization of the presynaptic plasma membrane, which is necessary to increase presynaptic calcium influx that drives enhanced neurotransmitter release during PHP.
claims.source: Increased levels of Shaker channel, which localizes to the presynaptic terminal at the NMJ (Figure 7), prevents ENaC channel-dependent depolarization of the presynaptic plasma membrane, which is necessary to increase presynaptic calcium influx that drives enhanced neurotransmitter release during PHP (Younger et al., 2013; Parrish et al., 2014; Orr et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Younger et al., 2013; Parrish et al., 2014; and Orr et al., 2017, and reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: Synapses in the pore-blocking ShalW362F mutant were capable of undergoing PHP.
claims.source: Decreased mEPSP amplitude was precisely offset by an increase in presynaptic release (quantal content, QC) that restored EPSP amplitudes to pre-PhTx amplitudes in both wild type and ShalW362F animals (Figure 7K & L). Thus, unlike in the protein null Shal495 mutant, synapses in the pore-blocking ShalW362F mutant were capable of undergoing PHP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K and L.

claims.claim: FRH can be induced and fully expressed in single, genetically identified neurons.
claims.source: First, we demonstrate that FRH can be induced and fully expressed in single, genetically identified neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing FRH in MN1.

claims.claim: Changes in the activity of a single motoneuron are unlikely to dramatically alter the behavior of the larvae.
claims.source: Since changes in the activity of a single motoneuron are unlikely to dramatically alter the behavior of the larvae, these data argue strongly for cell autonomous mechanisms that detect the presence of the ion channel perturbation and induce a corrective, homeostatic response.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design and results.

claims.claim: FRH functions to preserve the waveform of individual action potentials.
claims.source: Second, we demonstrate that FRH functions to preserve the waveform of individual action potentials.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing preserved AP waveform.

claims.claim: The transcription factor Krüppel is essential for FRH.
claims.source: Third, we provide new evidence that the transcription factor Krüppel is essential for FRH, and selectively controls the homeostatic enhancement of IKCA, without altering the baseline ion channel current.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing impaired FRH when Kr is knocked down.

claims.claim: Different mechanisms of FRH are induced depending upon how the Shal current is eliminated.
claims.source: Finally, we demonstrate that different mechanisms of FRH are induced depending upon how the Shal current is eliminated, and these differential expression mechanisms can have perturbation-specific effects on animal behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing Shal-RNAi and ShalW362F.

claims.claim: Parallel homeostatic mechanisms exist that are responsive to differential disruption of the Shal gene.
claims.source: We propose the existence of parallel homeostatic mechanisms, responsive to differential disruption of the Shal gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on speculation from the experimental results showing different compensatory responses.

claims.claim: Altered activity cannot be the sole determinant of FRH.
claims.source: First, altered activity cannot be the sole determinant of FRH. Two functionally identical manipulations that eliminate the Shal conductance, each predicted to have identical effects on neuronal excitability, lead to molecularly distinct homeostatic responses.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results comparing Shal-RNAi and ShalW362F.

claims.claim: Homeostatic signaling systems are sensitive to the type of mutation that affects an ion channel gene.
claims.source: Second, homeostatic signaling systems are sensitive to the type of mutation that affects an ion channel gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental results showing different responses to different Shal mutations.

claims.claim: Separable proteostatic and activity-dependent homeostatic signaling systems potentially act in concert to achieve cell-type-specific and perturbation-specific FRH.
claims.source: Finally, our data speak to experimental and theoretical studies arguing that the entire repertoire of ion channels encoded in the genome is accessible to the mechanisms of homeostatic feedback, with a very large combinatorial solution space (Marder and Prinz, 2002; O'Leary et al., 2014). Our data are consistent with the existence of separable proteostatic and activity-dependent homeostatic signaling systems, potentially acting in concert to achieve cell-type-specific and perturbation-specific FRH.

claims.claim: FRH has been widely documented within invertebrate neurons and neural circuits as well as the vertebrate spinal cord, cortical pyramidal neurons and cardiomyocytes.

results.result: MN1-GAL4 drives Shal-RNAi expression selectively in MN1 motoneurons, resulting in dramatic reduction of somatically measured IKA current. Wild-type MN1 shows IKA activation at approximately −30 mV reaching 20 pA/pF at +40 mV, while Shal-RNAi eliminates substantial current until +20 mV with only small residual outward current above this voltage.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C9 provide converging evidence from GAL4 expression patterns (C1), prior validation of the RNAi construct (C2), and direct electrophysiological measurements (C3-C5) demonstrating effective elimination of somatic IKA. The data are supported by both current measurements and comparison to prior characterization of Shal null mutants.

results.result: Acute pharmacological block of IKA with 4-AP significantly increases MN1 firing rates and causes depolarization block at high current steps, while chronic Shal knockdown maintains wild-type firing rates without depolarization block, demonstrating cell-autonomous firing rate homeostasis (FRH).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C16 demonstrate a clear differential effect between acute (4-AP) and chronic (Shal-RNAi) elimination of IKA. The acute condition increases firing and causes depolarization block (C10-C12), while chronic knockdown maintains normal firing (C13-C14), with 4-AP specificity confirmed (C15). This provides strong evidence for cell-autonomous FRH (C16).

results.result: FRH preserves action potential waveform following Shal knockdown. While acute 4-AP application reduces after-hyperpolarization amplitude, chronic Shal elimination maintains wild-type action potential characteristics including repolarization kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 and C20-C21 demonstrate preservation of AP waveform during FRH. The differential effects of acute versus chronic IKA elimination on AP parameters provide evidence for precise homeostatic compensation. Statistical comparisons support the conclusion that AP waveform is maintained despite loss of a major potassium conductance.

results.result: A CRISPR-engineered pore-blocking mutation (ShalW362F) eliminates IKA and induces robust FRH comparable to Shal-RNAi. The W362F mutation is a conserved pore-blocking substitution that traffics to the membrane, and ShalW362F mutants show normal firing rates that are insensitive to 4-AP.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 establish that FRH can be induced by eliminating Shal conductance without eliminating Shal protein. The pore-blocking mutation is validated by prior work (C22-C23), eliminates IKA (C24), and produces FRH equivalent to protein elimination (C25-C26). This demonstrates FRH can be triggered by loss of channel function (C27).

results.result: Shal knockdown induces compensatory increases in IKDR and IKCa currents without altering sodium or calcium currents. The elevated IKCa is primarily Slo-dependent, as demonstrated by virtual elimination in slo mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 document specific ionic conductance changes during FRH. The enhancement of IKDR and IKCa (C29, C34) with no change in INa or ICa (C30) is supported by voltage-clamp data. The Slo-dependence of IKCa is validated by slo mutant controls (C31) and prior transcript analysis (C32), though C33 acknowledges uncertainty about SK channel contribution.

results.result: The transcription factor Krüppel (Kr) is induced by loss of Shal and is required for FRH. Double knockdown of Shal and Kr significantly decreases firing rates compared to wild-type, while neither single knockdown alone alters baseline firing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 establish Kr as essential for FRH. Prior work shows Kr induction by Shal loss (C39-C41), and the current data demonstrate that Kr knockdown in the Shal-RNAi background impairs FRH (C42-C43). Critical controls show no baseline effects of either single knockdown (C44-C46), supporting the conclusion that Kr specifically mediates homeostatic compensation.

results.result: Kr controls homeostatic regulation of action potential waveform. While Shal-RNAi alone preserves wild-type AP waveform, double Shal-RNAi/Kr-RNAi significantly alters AP characteristics with reduced after-hyperpolarization and increased half-width.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 demonstrate Kr's role in AP waveform homeostasis. The preserved waveform in Shal-RNAi (C47) contrasts with altered waveform in double knockdown (C49-C50), with Kr-RNAi alone having no effect (C48). This supports the conclusion that Kr participates in homeostatic control of both firing rate and AP waveform (C51).

results.result: Post-mitotic Kr knockdown does not alter MN1 cell identity, morphology, or major passive electrical properties. Cell number, soma diameter, and dendrite width remain unchanged, though input resistance decreases in Kr-RNAi and double knockdown conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 address the concern that Kr knockdown might alter cell fate. Despite Kr's role in cell fate determination (C52), post-mitotic knockdown preserves cell number and morphology (C53-C54). The decreased input resistance (C55) is noted but does not account for the observed effects on firing rate and AP waveform, supporting the specificity of Kr's homeostatic role.

results.result: Double Shal-RNAi/Kr-RNAi shows the highest cell-to-cell variability in firing rates, particularly at current steps above 100 pA, though no individual cell fires at rates exceeding wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 provide evidence that Kr loss disrupts homeostatic control rather than establishing a new set point. The increased variability (C56) and constraint on maximal firing rates (C57) suggest impaired homeostasis rather than a shifted set point, though the authors acknowledge uncertainty about defining homeostatic set points.

results.result: Kr selectively controls homeostatic enhancement of IKCa without affecting baseline IKCa or calcium currents. Kr knockdown completely blocks the increase in IKCa following Shal loss, representing the first gene demonstrated to have selective action on homeostatic changes without altering baseline channel activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 establish Kr's selective role in IKCa homeostasis. The complete block of IKCa enhancement (C58) with no effect on baseline IKCa (C59) or calcium currents (C60) demonstrates specificity. The conclusion that Kr is the first gene with this selective homeostatic action (C62) is supported by the data, though it relies on the authors' knowledge of the field.

results.result: Kr does not control homeostatic upregulation of IKDR. IKDR remains elevated in double Shal-RNAi/Kr-RNAi similar to Shal-RNAi alone, and Kr knockdown has no effect on baseline IKDR.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 demonstrate that Kr's homeostatic role is specific to IKCa and does not extend to IKDR. The maintained IKDR elevation in double knockdown (C63) and lack of baseline effect (C65) support this conclusion. Control data showing equivalent IKA knockdown efficiency (C66) rules out technical artifacts.

results.result: Acute pharmacological inhibition of BK channels with paxilline significantly reduces firing rates in both wild-type and Shal-RNAi neurons, with effects on AP waveform consistent with double Shal-RNAi/Kr-RNAi. Loss of Slo-dependent repolarization leads to broader APs and shallower AHPs, impairing sodium channel recovery and decreasing firing rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 validate the role of IKCa in maintaining firing rates. Paxilline reduces firing by 34% (C69) compared to 12% with Kr knockdown (C70), consistent with Kr specifically regulating homeostatic IKCa enhancement. The AP waveform effects (C71) and mechanistic interpretation (C72) are supported by the data and known biophysical properties.

results.result: FRH is differentially achieved in ShalW362F compared to Shal-RNAi. ShalW362F shows upregulated IKDR but no change in IKCa, with no increase in Slo transcript and a small but significant AP broadening.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 demonstrate distinct homeostatic mechanisms downstream of different Shal perturbations. The upregulated IKDR (C73) without IKCa change (C74) contrasts with Shal-RNAi. The qPCR data showing no Slo transcript change (C76) versus upregulation in Shal null (C75) supports differential mechanisms. The small AP broadening (C77) is consistent with lack of IKCa compensation.

results.result: Gene expression changes differ between Shal null and ShalW362F mutants. While Krüppel, Shaker, slo, and Shab transcripts are elevated in Shal null mutants, none show altered expression in ShalW362F. Similarly, KCNQ, Shaw, and Shawl remain unchanged in ShalW362F despite KCNQ upregulation in Shal null.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 provide molecular evidence for distinct homeostatic responses. The qPCR data demonstrate clear differences in gene expression between Shal null (C79-C80, C83) and ShalW362F (C81-C82), supporting the conclusion that different perturbations to the same gene trigger different homeostatic mechanisms.

results.result: Motor behavior is differentially affected by different Shal perturbations. Wild-type and ShalW362F flies show normal climbing behavior, while pan-neuronal Shal knockdown dramatically impairs climbing. Motoneuron-specific Shal knockdown produces wild-type behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 demonstrate perturbation-specific effects on behavior. The normal behavior in ShalW362F (C84-C85) contrasts with impaired behavior in pan-neuronal Shal-RNAi (C86), with appropriate controls (C87-C88). This supports the conclusion that different homeostatic solutions have different functional consequences, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

results.result: Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is differentially affected by Shal perturbations. While Shal null mutants fail to express PHP due to increased Shaker expression blocking ENaC-dependent depolarization, ShalW362F mutants retain normal PHP capability.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 demonstrate perturbation-specific effects on synaptic plasticity. The prior work showing PHP blockade in Shal null (C89-C91) contrasts with preserved PHP in ShalW362F (C92). The electrophysiological data showing compensatory increase in quantal content support this conclusion, consistent with the lack of Shaker upregulation in ShalW362F.

results.result: The study demonstrates four key advances: (1) FRH can be induced and expressed in single neurons, (2) FRH preserves action potential waveform, (3) Krüppel is essential for FRH and selectively controls IKCa enhancement, and (4) different mechanisms of FRH are induced depending on how Shal is eliminated.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 summarize the major findings. Each conclusion is supported by the experimental data: single-neuron FRH (C93-C94), AP waveform preservation (C95), Kr's essential role (C96), and perturbation-specific mechanisms (C97). These represent the core contributions of the manuscript.

results.result: The authors propose parallel homeostatic mechanisms responsive to differential Shal disruption. Altered activity cannot be the sole determinant of FRH, homeostatic signaling is sensitive to mutation type, and separable proteostatic and activity-dependent systems may act in concert.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C101 represent interpretive conclusions and proposed models. While the data support the existence of different homeostatic responses (C99-C100), the proposal of parallel proteostatic and activity-dependent systems (C98, C101) is speculative. The model is consistent with the data but requires additional experimental validation to be fully supported.

results.result: The introduction establishes the context for FRH research, noting widespread documentation across systems, precise restoration of firing properties, limited mechanistic understanding, and current theories emphasizing calcium-dependent feedback. Questions remain about whether calcium is the only sensed variable and why homeostatic mechanisms fail in disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C109 accurately represent the state of the field based on cited literature. These claims establish the rationale for the study and are supported by appropriate citations. They represent background knowledge rather than new findings from this manuscript.

results.result: Prior characterization of Shal null mutants and pharmacological tools validates the current experimental approach. The Shal495 null shows a +50 mV voltage shift with remaining current from homeostatic Shaker upregulation in axonal membranes. 4-AP at 1-2 mM has reasonable specificity for IKA.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C19 cite prior work to validate experimental approaches. The characterization of Shal null mutants (C6-C7) and Shaker localization (C8) from prior studies support the interpretation of current data. The 4-AP specificity (C19) is appropriately qualified, acknowledging limitations while citing supporting evidence.

results.result: The hypothesis that FRH involves compensatory ion channel gene expression is supported by prior work. Changes in IKDR parallel those in mammalian Kv4.2 knockouts. IKDR can be encoded by four genes in Drosophila, with XE991 showing no differential effect on IKDR in Shal-RNAi.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C35-C38 establish the conceptual framework and provide comparative context. The hypothesis (C28) is supported by citations, the parallel to mammalian systems (C35) validates the findings, and the pharmacological test with XE991 (C37-C38) rules out KCNQ as the source of IKDR changes, though the data are not shown.
